intro: A warrior asks to see his friend as he truly is. A boy waits three nights at the door of Death. A father tells his son to break open a seed. These are scenes from the Bhagavad Gita and the Upanishads, and Hindus have returned to them for centuries in prayer, study and argument.

In this unit you will read the Gita's chapters on devotion (9 to 12) and its final teaching (18), then three Upanishads: the Katha, the Chandogya and the Isha. You will learn how devotion, awe and knowledge fit together in the Gita, and how the Upanishads teach through dialogues and simple images like salt, seeds and a chariot.

By the end you will be able to read a dialogue closely, name who asks and who answers, explain what image carries the idea, and describe how different Hindu schools have read the same words, such as tat tvam asi or Gita 18.66, without ranking them.
bigQuestion: How do the Gita and the Upanishads teach about the self, God and devotion, and why do their readers understand them differently?

test.q: What does Gita 9.26 name as offerings?
choices: A leaf, a flower, a fruit and water
test.why: 9.26 names simple offerings given with love.

test.q: What does Krishna give Arjuna so he can see the universal form?
test.why: Gita 11.8: ordinary eyes cannot see it.

test.q: What does Krishna call himself in Gita 11.32?
test.why: 11.32 is the Time verse; Yama is the teacher in the Katha.

test.q: Which chapter has the refrain "that devotee is dear to me"?
Which tradition calls Gita 18.66 the charama shloka?
test.why: Sri Vaishnavas, following Ramanuja, give 18.66 this name.

test.q: What are the three paths often found in the Gita?
Why are the Upanishads called Vedanta?
choices: They are part of the epics
They are the end or goal of the Veda
test.why: Vedanta means end of the Veda.

choices: To know what happens after death
test.why: The Katha Upanishad centers on this question.

test.q: What is the difference between shreyas and preyas?
test.why: Katha 1.2: shreyas is the good; preyas the pleasant.

test.q: In Katha 1.3.3, what is the body?
test.why: The body is the chariot; the self is the rider.

test.q: In Chandogya 6, what is the lesson of the salt?
choices: The essence is present everywhere, though unseen
test.why: The salt pervades the water and is known by taste.

test.q: How do Advaita and other Vedanta schools differ on tat tvam asi?
choices: Other schools say it is a later Buddhist addition
They all read it the same way
Advaita reads identity of self and Brahman; others read dependence or relation
test.why: The phrase is read as identity by Advaita and as relation by other schools.

choices: Enjoy by renouncing and do not covet
test.why: Isha 1 pairs letting go with not coveting.

test.q: Whose wording is "Now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds"?
test.why: Oppenheimer used his own rendering of Gita 11.32.

choices: The son taught by Uddalaka in Chandogya 6
test.why: Shvetaketu is Uddalaka's son; Nachiketa meets Yama.

write.prompt: Do the Gita and the Upanishads picture the path to the highest goal in the same way? Cite two or three passages (for example Gita 9.26 or 18.66, Katha 1.3.3, Chandogya 6.13; give the translation), explain what each says, and describe how at least two schools of readers have understood them.
tips: Name the text, chapter and verse, and the translation you used.
Say who is speaking and to whom in each passage.
Attribute every reading: "Advaita teachers read…", "Sri Vaishnavas read…".
Use the unit's terms: bhakti, Brahman, tat tvam asi, marga.
